name: Douglas Carswell
subject: The Midterms – What to Make of Them?
body:
| | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/mspolicy/midterms?e=5703353baa)
---
| |
---
| _**If you're not in front of our Saturday email, you're behind.**_
---
| Dear Friend,
So. Tariffs. Not so great, eh?

I think America has just given the world a pretty good demonstration of why tariffs are a very bad idea, both economically and politically.

Two years ago, Donald Trump was reelected, carrying every one of the swing states. He beat Kamala Harris, standing in for an administration widely blamed for soaring inflation and the rising cost of gas and groceries.

Yet within weeks of taking office, Trump slapped tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China, then on steel, aluminum and cars. On "Liberation Day" in April 2025, he hit almost every country, friend and foe alike, with tariffs of 10 to 50 per cent.

Tariffs, some said at the time, were all about taking on China. In which case, why, for heaven’s sake were they applied on imports from Canada?

Of course, it was neither Canadians nor Chinese that paid the tariffs. It was the American consumer. The National Taxpayers Union estimated a few months back that tariffs are costing US consumers around $200 billion a year. A basket of everyday back-to-school supplies is now $147 more expensive than before due to tariffs.

We know beyond doubt that tariffs were the key issue in the midterm election because the exit polls tell us so. Most voters said tariffs had hurt the economy. According to an NBC exit poll, about two thirds said the President’s policies had made it worse.

"But what about the Iran war?" some will ask. "Surely that played a part?"

It did, but it doesn't let tariffs off the hook. It made the damage worse. Launched with little thought for the consequences, the war choked off oil shipments from the Gulf for months. Gas prices soared, and so did the cost of essentials such as fertilizer. Voters already squeezed by tariffs were squeezed again.

No state shows more vividly the part tariffs played in the Republicans’ midterm disaster than our own. Mississippi has just gone and elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1982.

The defeated incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, was an unequivocal champion of tariffs – at least initially. “I think that it’s a really good tool,” she once said. “The president knows how to use that tool.”

Her victorious opponent, Scott Colom, was anti-tariff — consistently, repeatedly and relentlessly. “The tariffs are a sales tax,” he told voters. “They’re a tax on everything.”

In Mississippi, the Democrat ran as a free trader — and won.

Most Americans – in this state and beyond - have worked out that tariffs make them poorer. If you still doubt it, stand in Kroger and admire one of those $20 bags of ground coffee. When I moved here six years ago, they cost around $11.

In the summer of 2025, Washington slapped a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian coffee. Who was it meant to protect? Mississippi has no coffee farmers. Apart from a handful of growers in Hawaii, neither does America. A little over three months later, the White House quietly dropped the tariff on coffee — which was as good as admitting that the tariff was being paid by ordinary American households.

Much of the damage done by tariffs could not so easily be undone. Mississippi’s soybean crop is worth around $1.6 billion a year, and almost all of it is sold abroad – at one time mostly to China.

When tariffs triggered a trade war, Beijing stopped buying American soybeans. It placed no orders for much of last year. Guess who filled the gap? Brazil. A market Mississippi farmers had spent decades building was handed to their biggest competitor. Even after a trade deal, China’s purchases are about half what they were.

It gets worse. That same summer, Washington put a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian beef, just as American beef prices were already soaring. The White House dropped that too within months – again an admission that it was American households paying. But the damage was done.

A pound of ground beef cost $6.76 last month. Five years ago, it was $4.72. “Shhhhiiiii”, one might say.
“Hold on!” I hear you wondering, “Why not feed our own soybeans to our own cattle, and stop relying on foreigners for either?”

Some 250 years ago, Adam Smith showed that nations grow rich by buying from others what those others make more cheaply. If that lesson has not yet reached policymakers, let me put it more bluntly.

Try telling a Mississippi mom at the checkout, worried if she’s enough on her card, that self-sufficiency is in the interests of her family, as you make her pay more for less. You might as well be telling her to go “pick another protein.”

To be fair to Cindy Hyde-Smith, she never actually said “pick another protein”, and in my view a fair amount of the campaign coverage was unfair to her.

When farmers complained about the cost of fertilizer, she went to the White House and fixed it by having the tariffs on it lifted. The same order also scrapped tariffs on beef and coffee.

But if tariffs are bad for Mississippi farmers when they buy fertilizer, why are they good for anyone else? It was another quiet admission of who pays — clear for anyone with eyes to see, long before election disaster the other day.

And it really was a disaster for the Republican Party. Texas has elected its first Democratic governor since 1990. Georgia elected Democrats to every statewide office. Kansas has sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 94 years.

Democrats now hold at least 55 seats in the Senate. They are still short of the two thirds needed to override a presidential veto. Even so, I suspect that for the next two years it will often feel as if the Democrats are in power but not in office, while the Republicans are in office but not in power.

My greater fear, however, is that people will draw the wrong lessons.

Already there is pressure on the President to back off enforcing the law on illegal immigration. If the deportation agenda loses momentum, America risks starting to look like parts of Europe a few years down the line. A robust approach on immigration is the glue that has held the conservative coalition together. Go soft on that, and American conservatives will end up in as sorry a state as British ones.

I fear something similar regarding data centers. Republicans did badly despite being on the right side of that argument, not because of it. If the party now reads the result as a verdict against growth, it will throw away the one thing that can bring bills down — more investment, more jobs and more energy.

Voters did not reject conservatism. They rejected a tariff policy that made them poorer. The answer to that is not less free enterprise. It is more.

Perhaps there is one silver lining. Mississippi competes with other states for jobs, investment and people. If Texas and Georgia now choose to be governed like California, we have a chance to double down on a pro growth agenda.

Washington sets tariffs. Jackson can do a whole raft of things that make us more competitive. We cannot undo the damage done by bad federal policy, but we can make Mississippi the place where it pays to work, build and invest. Get rid of the income tax. Say yes to new investment. Go all in on affordable energy.

States that turn their backs on growth lose. Let’s make sure Mississippi is the one that gains.

On Friday, October 23, 2026, federal prosecutors in Chicago announced that Parth Nayi, of Woodridge, had been sentenced to two years in prison and a $50,000 fine by U.S. District Judge Mary M. Rowland. Nayi pleaded guilty earlier this year to conspiracy to commit visa fraud. Prosecutors say he staged _hundreds_ of fake armed robberies across the country so that participants could claim to be crime victims on U-visa applications -- and that each participant paid him between $5,000 and $30,000 for the service (DOJ; FOX 32).
The scheme, step by step. The Chicago case broke open May 17, 2024, when prosecutors charged six men -- based in Woodridge, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, Wisconsin and Florida -- with staging holdups in and around the city; a June 2024 indictment listed robberies in Elmwood Park and River Grove (Tribune). The indictment catalogued more than a dozen venues: gas stations in Lombard and Hickory Hills; Subway restaurants in Chicago, Elmwood Park and Louisiana; a Tropical Smoothie Cafe in St. Charles; multiple Dunkin Donuts stores in Chicago and South Holland; liquor stores in Chicago, River Grove and Lake Villa; a 7-Eleven; a truck stop in Tennessee (CBS Chicago). name: James Talarico
subject: Go big or go home
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Talarico for Texas
body:
#
Peter —
As I walked the halls of the United States Senate during our orientation earlier this week, Lyndon B. Johnson was everywhere — busts, portraits, plaques. It felt like he was speaking to me as I prepared to take back his Senate seat.
I think LBJ has something to say to all of us in this moment.
LBJ married two things that are at odds in the modern Democratic Party: the practical politics of coalition-building and a bold moral imagination.
LBJ’s Great Society was not just a legislative agenda; it was a vision. It was a dream. An America where everyone can fulfill their God-given potential. A beloved community. A more perfect union.
And he passed an agenda worthy of that dream: Head Start, Title 1, Medicare, Medicaid, public television, the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, fair housing, space exploration, the War on Poverty, the National Endowment for the Arts, highway beautification.
Everything is bigger in Texas — including our policy ambitions. In Texas, we go big, or we go home.
So here’s what I told Democrats gathered for a post-midterm debrief about we need to do with our Texas-sized mandate:
* We must get Big Money out of our politics so no billionaire — or trillionaire — can buy our elections.
* We must ban gerrymandering nationwide — in red states and blue states alike.
* We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%.
* We must pass universal healthcare so no one goes bankrupt just because they get sick.
* We must invest in our teachers and our students and build an American public education system that is the envy of the world.
* We must overhaul this broken immigration system and build a pathway to citizenship for our neighbors who have been here for years.
* We must cut red tape and build millions of new homes so every American can realize the dream of homeownership.
* We must regulate artificial intelligence, crack down on data centers, and pass an AI Dividend so every American has a share in this AI future.
* We must end these forever wars that are driving up prices and champion a new, values-based foreign policy.

As we look ahead to January, as we look ahead to the next couple of years, we need to summon the ambition of LBJ.
The American people want change, and in this election, they gave our party a chance to deliver it.
We can’t let them down.
We can’t play it safe.
We can’t get bogged down in petty fights.
We can’t settle for nibbling around the edges or results people will only feel a decade from now.
We need to be brave. We need to be bold. We need to be big. We need a Democratic Party that’s a little less Washington, and a little more Texas.
In the words of Thomas Paine: “We have it in our power to begin the world over again."
We can write the next chapter of our history. We can remake our country. We can build a new Great Society.
It’s time to go big or go home.
James
The fights ahead will not be easy. Billionaires and corporate interests spent record-breaking sums to try to defeat our movement in Texas. The status quo is not done fighting back to keep the system rigged.

We must overhaul this broken immigration system and build a pathway to citizenship for our neighbors who have been here for years. We must cut red tape and build millions of new homes so every American can realize the dream of homeownership. We must regulate artificial intelligence, crack down on data centers, and pass an AI Dividend so every American has a share in this AI future. We must end these forever wars that are driving up prices and champion a new, values-based foreign policy. As we look ahead to January, as we look ahead to the next couple of years, we need to summon the ambition of LBJ. The American people want change, and in this election, they gave our party a chance to deliver it. We can’t let them down. We can’t play it safe. We can’t get bogged down in petty fights. We can’t settle for nibbling around the edges or results people will only feel a decade from now. We need to be brave. We need to be bold. We need to be big. We need a Democratic Party that’s a little less Washington, and a little more Texas. In the words of Thomas Paine: “We have it in our power to begin the world over again." We can write the next chapter of our history. We can remake our country. We can build a new Great Society. It’s time to go big or go home. James The fights ahead will not be easy. Billionaires and corporate interests spent record-breaking sums to try to defeat our movement in Texas. The status quo is not done fighting back to keep the system rigged. ** Paid for by Talarico for Texas Talarico for Texas PO Box 14508 Austin, TX 78761

name: Kristen McDonald Rivet
subject: How we did it (again)
body:
|
#
Friend, Two years ago, we won a district President Trump carried by 2 points. When people asked how we did it, I told them the answer was simple: we did things differently. Well, we did it again this election. And the answer hasn’t changed. **Here’s what you need to know:**
* We won by 14 points in one of the most competitive districts in the country – despite millions in outside spending.
* Our campaign showed the strongest crossover appeal of any Democratic House candidate in Michigan.
* Every corner of this district moved our way compared to 2024: Flint, Saginaw, Bay City, and Midland too.

[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/143450217/660253151/-185804088?refcode=em-11.14.26-all&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzMvMS85NjAyNCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI2ZjlkOGQ2MC00MmUwLWYxMTEtOTFmMC0wMDBkM2ExOGUyNDQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=VyhIBI3sP8SXq1jx1IqpekkjQi0CY0jgsUhRrNfmD-4=) None of that happened by accident, friend. Our team spent this cycle on front porches all across the district – in fact, we knocked on 200,000 doors. We talked about what people here actually lose sleep over: being able to work one job and build a middle-class life, the cost of child care and prescription drugs, and protecting fundamental rights. And in this election, voters could see what I’d done in Congress. When Elon Musk tried to shut down Saginaw’s Social Security office, we rallied the community and saved it. Working families on SNAP still can’t buy a hot rotisserie chicken at the grocery store, so I got a bill through the House to change that – and I won’t stop until it’s law. Two years ago, I said I wasn’t going to play by Washington’s rules. I meant it. And mid-Michigan noticed. Now, with a Democratic majority, we finally have the chance to deliver on more of what voters have been asking for: lower costs, affordable health care, and a government that works for _you,_ not special interests. More soon, Kristen | ** 👋 Before you go...** Holding this seat wasn’t cheap. Outside groups poured millions into trying to defeat us, and we had to spend big to fight back. Unfortunately, we expect Republicans to make this one of their top targets again in 2028.

A federal judge ruled Friday that the Hermon School Department violated The Pines Church's rights under the First Amendment and the Maine Human Rights Act when it denied the church a year-long lease of school facilities.
Chief U.S. District Judge Lance E. Walker issued the [37-page Decision and Order](https://substack.com/redirect/948b7072-3a6e-4667-aff9-7ea9f931b544?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) after a two-day bench trial in the lawsuit brought by the church and its lead pastor, Matt Gioia. Walker entered a declaratory judgment that the department's treatment and denial of the church's application for a year-long lease violated those rights.
The Maine Wire first broke the story about the discriminatory actions of the Hermon School Department -- and ex-school board member Christopher McLaughlin, in particular -- back in 2023 when it obtained emails via the Freedom of Access Act showing McLaughlin attempting to impose a religious litmus test on who would be allowed to rent public spaces controlled by the school system.
You can count on the liberal media to expose stories like this. Or you can support The Robinson Report.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..TjTTMghB9fQ9F5Kk75TEYgRay36HdxcCda5HHKyY5qo?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=224822561)
In response to the Christian church's request to rent the school gymnasium, McLaughlin sent an email to Superintendent Micah Grant demanding that Gioia explain what the church teaches about transvestites, whether boys can become girls, abortion, birth control, and genital mutilation for young people.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d232c8db-854d-488a-bbcc-567b00541baf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The obvious implication of McLaughlin's email was that if the Christian pastor taught Christian beliefs at his Christian church, then McLaughlin would use his position of power to discriminate against the lease request on the basis of those religious beliefs.
He resigned in 2024 when Pines Church sued over the attempted religious discrimination. Two years later, the blatant act of anti-Christian bigotry has finally been confirmed by a federal judge.
Walker found it more likely than not that "discriminatory animus toward the Church" motivated the department to decline the year-long lease. Under the Maine Human Rights Act, he found that "the Church's status was a substantial factor in the Committee's decision not to lease to the Church for their requested lease term." He wrote of "undertones and overtones of bad motive unabated throughout the decision-making process."
McLaughlin has previously served as the Associate Vice President of Community and Pediatric Services at Northern Light Acadia Hospital in Bangor and Executive Director of the National Association of Social Workers (NASW) Maine Chapter. He has also served on the Maine Board of Social Work Licensing and on boards for the Maine Children's Alliance and a Diversity Hiring Coalition.
Although Walker ruled in favor of Pines Church, he denied the church's request for an injunction. He awarded the church and Gioia $1 in nominal damages (court-ordered) and reasonable costs. Attorney fees have not yet been determined.
At its December 12, 2022, meeting, the Hermon School Committee did not take a vote on the church's request for a year-long lease of the theater, cafeteria and classrooms at Hermon High School for Sunday morning services. Vice Chair Shorey moved a six-month lease. The motion failed for lack of a second. Member Stephanie Oiler then moved a month-to-month lease, which passed 4-1. Chair Jesse Keith, Shorey, Oiler and Haily Keezer voted yes. Christopher McLaughlin voted no.
Gioia rejected the month-to-month offer, as he'd previously explained to the board that a month-to-month arrangement was not tenable for the church's long-term planning. Conservative critics at the time called the purported compromise a bad-faith attempt to cover up for McLaughlin's outed animus.
Walker agreed. He wrote that the committee knew the church needed a more fixed arrangement, and that the month-to-month offer "appears to me to have been an offer designed to be rejected not one born of wholesome support for the Free Exercise Clause." He did not order the department to grant a longer lease.
Walker found that at least three of the committee's five voting members acted under the influence of bad motive: McLaughlin, Oiler and Shorey.
He wrote, "I find without any difficulty that McLaughlin exhibited bad motive," and that McLaughlin's "intrusive questions expressed viewpoint related concerns towards Plaintiffs."
In addition to the questions McLaughlin put in writing to the superintendent, the LGBTQ activist also interrogated Gioia at an in-person meeting. At the church's November 7, 2022, presentation, McLaughlin asked about the church's denomination.
Grant forwarded the questions to Gioia on November 10.
Gioia did not answer them.
Instead, he responded in a November 28 letter that it is "entirely inappropriate for a representative of the State (the school board) to ask a religious organization about their faith, morality, and political stances, when considering them for a lease or for any other matter."
Oiler raised concerns about crowd size, parking, staffing and cleaning. Walker wrote that the members' concerns were "definitively dispelled" by Grant, and that "Oiler's attitude toward the Church was anything but neutral." He found that "Oiler's chief concern was that the tenant would be a Church."
Walker credited Grant, who testified that he is a born-again Christian, with "acting as a guardrail" when the committee "started to drive the process into a constitutional bridge abutment." He wrote that "Grant's conduct as to procedure supported and favored treating the Church equally to all other potential public users of public space."
[Share The Robinson Report](https://substack.com/redirect/d02501dd-83ee-44e4-8fd7-e5167ef223b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Grant announced his [resignation in April 2024](https://substack.com/redirect/e0f16e40-dcee-4374-830c-82053be8c926?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), citing personal reasons.
The department has said the church was treated like other community groups. Its attorney, Melissa Hewey of far-left law firm Drummond Woodsum, argued at a June 2024 hearing that the church was allowed to use the facility and simply was not granted a year-long lease. The opinion records Grant telling the committee that this was the first year-long lease request it had received. Walker wrote that "novelty is not a basis to discriminate against religious organizations."
McLaughlin, Oiler and Shorey -- the three school board members found to have acted out of bad-faith animus toward Christians -- won't suffer any financial penalty for the attempted discrimination, as the taxpayers cover the costs of Drummond Woodsum's LGBTQ advocacy in schools.
The Pines Church case is oddly similar to another instance of anti-Christian bigotry from a separate taxpayer-funded institution: the University of Maine System.
[[RELATED: UMaine Rescinds Offer to Sell Hutchinson Center to Belfast Church...]](https://substack.com/redirect/d5d36a96-6c7f-489e-b85a-f531d25d6eff?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
In 2024, after Calvary Chapel Belfast won the bid to purchase the system's Hutchinson Center to serve as its new church, UMS caved to pressure from left-wing activists and [reneged](https://substack.com/redirect/d5d36a96-6c7f-489e-b85a-f531d25d6eff?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on the sale.

clean_body: | ~ | | Peter, I understand that organizers don’t have unlimited resources. I understand that sometimes, we have to make tough calls. I understand that big dreams take time to achieve. But I will never understand how anyone could look me in the eyes and tell me that my home state – and everyone living there – isn’t “worth” fighting for. Still, people always ask why we’re so invested in organizing across Florida. They claim that Florida is too red, too far gone, too deep under the thumb of the far-right fascists like Ron DeSantis, and that we can’t “afford” to fight back. If I’d listened to that kind of defeatism in 2022, I wouldn’t be writing to you today as the first Gen Z member of Congress. And I’m damn sure not listening to it in 2026. ~ | | ~ Thanks to people like you, chipping in spare change and sometimes digging even deeper, we’ve gained ground in Florida. This state is in play, and you won’t catch me on the sidelines when everything from our education to our democracy to our planet’s survival is at stake. Now, I’m not gonna sugarcoat what we’re really up against. It’s true that Floridians have been subjected to far-right policies for years, and that it’s caused real suffering. It’s true that billionaire weirdos have been funding fascism here for even longer. But that’s exactly why we have to organize and fight back. If we don’t advocate for a better future, we accept the one Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans are trying to carve out for us. Friend, my message to party leadership is simple: Don’t just talk about a majority, show us what a majority can do. Don’t just talk about healthcare justice, pass Medicare for All. Don’t just talk about abortion justice, pass national abortion protections. Don’t just talk about Black lives mattering, enact reparations now. Don’t just talk about ending ICE’s terror, take every last dollar from them and abolish ICE. We have the power, and now we have to actually use it. **This is all possible with our hard-fought victories. And we owe it to voters to deliver.** Now is not the time to moderate our aspirations. # How to Unsend an Email on iPhone After You’ve Sent It
Have you ever tapped send and immediately realized something was wrong with your email? We've all been there. You can unsend an email on your iPhone or iPad if you realize your mistake within a set amount of time. This can save you a lot of embarrassment and the pain of having to write a follow-up correction email.
## Why You’ll Love This Tip
* **Learn how to take back an email you wish you hadn’t sent.**
* **Avoid conflict, confusion, or embarrassment by unsending emails.**
* **Change the timeframe you have to unsend emails, from 10 seconds up to 30 seconds.**

## How to Recall and Email Sent on iPhone & iPad
### System Requirements
_This tip works on iPhones running iOS 16 or later, and was tested on an iPhone 17 Pro running iOS 26.4. Find out how to update to[the latest version of iOS](https://click.iphonelife.com/ga/click/2-17209627-5-0-260936-8633304-eb261b4cda-ejbc834839)._If you change your mind after tapping send on an email, you can unsend the email on your iPad or iPhone. If you wish to unsend an email that you sent via the Mail app, you have [up to 30 seconds](href=) to do so.Note: If you delete an email, does it unsend? The answer is no. The recipient still receives and keeps the email even if you delete it on your end. Using the Undo Send Delay feature is the only way to recall an email sent once you've hit the send icon.
1. Open the **Mail app** on your iPhone.

|
---
2. Draft an email and select a recipient, then tap the **Send icon**.

---
3. Tap the **Undo Send button** at the top of the Inbox to stop the email from sending.

---
### Enjoying Your Tip of the Day?
If you'd like to learn more about iPhone Life's premium paid subscription, [click here](https://click.iphonelife.com/ga/click/2-17209627-5-0-260936-8633305-2dbe5f5e1d-ejbc834839)

After you stop the email from sending, your Mail app will open the draft again, so you can edit it and resend if necessary.
If you wait longer than 10 seconds, you won’t be able to unsend the email unless you change the Mail Undo Send Delay in your settings. You can unsend an email regardless of whether the recipient has an iPhone or is running the latest software.
### How to Change the Mail Undo Send Delay Time
If you’d like to give yourself some more time to unsend an email, you can do so in the settings:
1. Open the **Settings app.**

---
2. Tap **Apps.**

---
3. Tap **Mail**.

---
4. Scroll to the bottom and tap **Undo Send Delay**.

---
5. Here you can pick between Off, 10 Seconds, 20 Seconds, and 30 Seconds. Tap one to select it.

---

I like to set my unsend email time limit to 30 seconds because it usually takes me a while to realize I made a mistake, so the more time I have, the better.
